speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, February 13, 1957, commemorates the 10th anniversary of a significant step in the development of our mineral resources, the discovery of petroleum near Leduc in Alberta. The intensified search for oil which followed this discovery has resulted in the spectacular growth of Canada's petroleum production from 20,000 barrels a day in 1946 to 467,000 barrels a day in 1956.
I think it is fitting that we pay tribute to those in private industry and government services whose foresight and tenacity have made possible this remarkable achievement and the opening up of important new areas of this country for development and production. These ten years of industrial achievement have added greatly to our national energy reserves, as well as bringing closer the day when Canada will be self-sufficient in petroleum and natural gas.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED VARIATIONS IN BENEFIT PAYMENTS TO RAILWAYMEN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED VARIATIONS IN BENEFIT PAYMENTS TO RAILWAYMEN
speechtext:
On Thursday, February 7, the hon. member for Peterborough drew to my attention a letter published in the press concerning the varying amounts of benefit paid to railway employees as a result of layoffs occasioned by the recent strike. The varying amounts of benefit paid to employees having the same rates of wages are due to two factors-the rate of benefit authorized and the earnings during the two weeks of the layoff.
The differences in the benefit rates authorized arise from the fact that two persons having the same wage rates do not necessarily have the same earnings; and, as contributions are based on earnings, the rates of benefit are not identical. One person may have had time off for illness or other reasons, whilst the other had full-time employment. One might have had overtime and the other straight time, and so on. This, of course, affected the earnings, which was in turn reflected in the rate of benefit when a claim was made.
Regarding the variations in the amounts of benefit received due to earnings during the weeks of layoff, somewhat the same circumstances prevailed. Some employees worked or had earnings for one day in the week of December 30, 1956, the first week in which the layoff occurred; others had two days' earnings; whilst yet others had three and four days' earnings. Again, in the week of January 6, 1957, which is the week in which the strike ended, some men went back to work on Friday, others on Saturday, and the bulk on the following Monday or Tuesday. The earnings of a claimant during a calendar week must be taken into account in determining the amount of benefit to which he is entitled for that week-the benefit being reduced when the earnings exceed the amount permitted.

Inquiries of the Ministry
It is, therefore, largely because of the varying amounts of earnings both prior to and during the two weeks of the layoff that misunderstandings have arisen. This has been explained to officers of the railway brotherhoods, who have expressed satisfaction with the explanations given.
To clarify what I know has sounded like a very involved matter, I think it might help if I could place on Hansard some detailed information that has been prepared, together with schedules indicating how the amounts of benefit paid have been arrived at.
If I have permission to do that I shall be glad if it could be printed as part of my answer.

maintopic: DISQUALIFICATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY FIREMEN AND ENGINEERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: DISQUALIFICATION OF CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY FIREMEN AND ENGINEERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, could I have permission to reply to a question which has not been asked in the house but which a number of members on both sides of the house have asked me, having to do with disqualification under the Unemployment Insurance Act of firemen and engineers arising out of the strike on the Canadian Pacific Railway?
Disqualifications were imposed on all firemen and all engineers of the C.P.R. in respect of the recent labour dispute under section 63 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which reads as follows. I think I have to read this extract, sir, to make my reply adequate:
63. (1) An insured person who has lost his employment by reason of a stoppage of work attributable to a labour dispute at the factory, workshop or other premises at which he was employed, is disqualified from receiving benefit until
(a)	the termination of the stoppage of work,
(b)	he becomes bona fide employed elsewhere in the occupation that he usually follows, or
(c)	he has become regularly engaged in some other occupation,
whichever event first occurs.
(2) An insured person is not disqualified under this section if he proves that
(a)	he is not participating in, or financing or directly interested in the labour dispute that caused the stoppage of work, and
(b)	he does not belong to a grade or class of workers that, immediately before the commencement of the stoppage, included members who were employed at the premises at which the stoppage is taking place and are participating in, financing or directly interested in the dispute.
(3 Where separate branches of work that are commonly carried on as separate businesses in separate premises are carried on in separate departments on the same premises, each department shall, for the purpose of this section, be deemed to be a separate factory or workshop.
Under subsection 2 of this section a claimant who has lost his employment owing to a labour dispute is disqualified from the receipt of benefit for so long as the stoppage of work continues unless he proves that (a) he is not participating in, or financing or directly interested in the dispute; and (b) he is not a member of a grade or class of workers, any of whom are participating in, financing or directly interested in the dispute.
Under the collective bargaining agreements between the respective brotherhoods and the

railway, determination of whether an employee is a fireman or an engineer is made on what he was doing at 12.01 a.m. on the first day of each month. This basis was used by the unemployment insurance commission and the status as at January 1, 1957, so established.
Those who were classed as firemen on this basis were disqualified as participating, and being directly interested, in the dispute.
It was found that some engineers who are members of the firemen's brotherhood and are office bearers of that body pay full union dues to the firemen's brotherhood even when acting as engineers. As the strike pay disbursed to the firemen was paid from a fund to which these engineers were contributing they were considered as financing the dispute and so were disqualified. Since there were some engineers, members of the firemen's brotherhood, who thus financed the dispute then all of the engineers, because they belong to the same grade or class of workers as those financing, were subject to disqualification. It is understood that some 3,300 engineers were involved. Officials of the unemployment insurance commission have discussed the decision to disqualify the engineers with representatives of the railway brotherhood concerned and the latter have intimated their intention to appeal the decision to the board of referees and the umpire.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON APPOINTMENT OF LIEUTENANT GENERAL HANS SPEIDEL AS COMMANDER OF LAND FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) addressed the following question to the Prime Minister:
Was the Canadian government consulted concerning the appointment of Lieutenant General Hans Speidel as commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization central European land forces? If so, did the government express its approval of this appointment?

Inquiries of the Ministry
The answer to both questions is yes. On January 4 a message was received from General Norstad of NATO, the supreme allied commander, Europe, stating that the post of commanding general, allied land forces, central Europe, had been vacated by General Marcel Carpentier of the French army, and that the minister of defence of France, in concert with his Belgian and Netherlands colleagues, was proposing that the post should be allocated to a German officer of appropriate rank and experience. As Minister of National Defence I indicated approval in principle on behalf of Canada.
On January 24 General Norstad informed me that the West German national authorities, on being consulted, had nominated Lieutenant General Hans Speidel for the position. Canada, like all the other NATO countries concerned, agreed to the appointment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

speechtext:
Right Hon.	L.	S. St.	Laurent	(Prime
Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 47, for the establishment of a Canada Council for the encouragement of the arts, humanities and social sciences.
He said: Mr. Speaker, you will have seen from the Hansard	reports	that we	had incommittee on	the	resolution quite	a protracted and very interesting discussion of the general purposes of the legislation to be introduced following the resolution, and I do not think I could say anything at this time on the general purposes of the legislation that would not be a repetition of what I said at the resolution stage. When the bill, the general principles of which seemed to meet with very wide approval by the house, is before the committee I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen will wish to give very careful consideration to the various provisions of the bill and at that time I will endeavour to answer any questions that they may feel arise out of the various provisions contained in the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of fhe Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime
Minister has stated at the resolution stage, the principle of the resolution, and now of the bill before the house, met with general acceptance. We of the official opposition indicated our support for the principle of the bill and for the setting up of the Canada Council. However, there were one or two matters upon which we made suggestions and upon a perusal of the bill we find that those suggestions have in no way been accepted, particularly the suggestion of the hon. member for Vaneouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) that provision should be made in the bill for an examination by parliament.
When the matter was before the committee I referred to the fact that in general the

resolution, and now the bill, follow the line indicated by the Massey commission except in one major particular, the degree to which parliamentary control has not been assured either by the representations made by the Prime Minister during debate on the resolution or in the bill itself. At the expense of reiterating what I said previously, I again bring to the attention of the house the recommendation of that commission as set out on page 382 of their report. The commission said:
The development of the council's work would naturally depend upon the extent to which it would he able to satisfy with wisdom and moderation a real public need, and, if successful in this, we do not doubt that there would be public support of parliamentary action in making adequate funds available to it. We do not find it possible to propose specific sums; we should, however, imagine that the council would find it possible to perform its varied duties effectively with an annual budget which would constitute a very slight charge upon all members of the Canadian population.
Had provision been made to incorporate in the bill this major recommendation of the commission there would have been preserved to parliament its right to an examination of the disposition made of the funds voted by parliament, whether through the medium of endowments or through annual grants. Again, I repeat that the commission made the point that it would be dangerous if this Canada Council became in any sense a department of government, and went on to say:
. . . but we realize that since this body will be spending public money it must be in an effective manner responsible to the government and hence to parliament.
In the United Kingdom they have had experience with a similar council and I have before me the report of the first ten years. At page 16 the following appears:
The grant which parliament annually votes to the arts council is determined by several procedural checks. The council each year presents the chancellor with an itemized account of the subsidies which it believes necessary for maintaining the many organizations it supports. These figures are further examined in the treasury and finally, by a process more usually subject to subtraction than addition, the art council is voted a grant for the year.
Then it goes on to point out that while it was hoped at one time that there might be a quinquennial grant the country's fortunes have obstructed that aspiration. However, whether it be an annual grant or a quinquennial grant, the fact remains that there is a control on the expenditures made by that council in Britain which I believe should be incorporated in the bill now before us. As things now stand, there is nothing

whatsoever in the bill to maintain parliamentary control over the moneys of the Canadian people to be expended by the council to be set up.
I realize I am not permitted to refer to the sections of the bill by number, but there is only one provision that even in the slightest degree maintains anything in the nature of parliamentary responsibility over the moneys that are to be expended.
The only provision is simply that within three months after the termination of each fiscal year there is to be submitted to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated for the purpose a report of all proceedings, including the financial statements of the council and the Auditor General's report thereon. Then it goes on to indicate that the report shall be laid before parliament within 15 days after the receipt thereof or, if parliament is not then sitting, within 15 days next thereafter. In other words, there is merely a formality provided for. A tremendous amount of money is being placed in the hands of the council independent of parliament. In no portion of the bill that is before us is there anything to assure and maintain the right of parliament to an examination of the disposal made of the moneys voted by parliament.
In the second place, under the investments section there is nothing to prevent the Canada Council from investing in common stocks. I know there are some who believe that the provision for investment has its beneficial aspects in that, if common stocks were purchased on a rising market, the amount of the endowment would be greatly increased, nonetheless, the experience of Canadians and in particular the experience of one insurance company in the late twenties must place Canadians on guard against the danger of these moneys being invested by the council in common stock. Under the bill as it is now before the house, what control is there to deny to the council the opportunity to make expenditures which are dangerous and improvident. They are dangerous and improvident not because of the condition of the companies in which the investments are made at the time but dangerous in so far as future probabilities are concerned. I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) whether or not, even at this date, consideration should not be given to assuring that the moneys placed in the hands of this council shall be expended in a manner maintained by the responsibility of the council to parliament in an annual examination of the accounts of that council.
No one suggests that the personnel of the council may not be of the highest. Everyone expects that the members chosen shall
Canada Council
be above any suggestion of political partisanship. Yet for some reason the Prime Minister has not seen fit to give to the house and the country that assurance. When day by day press references lead us to believe that the identity of the chairman is already assured, I think that we have the right to ask that the Prime Minister today reveal to the house in committee whom he has in mind for this appointment and not leave it to the conjecture of press dispatches. If the person in question is the one he has in mind, regardless of the high regard that I have for that gentleman may I say that the Canada Council is, I believe, entitled to have as its chairman someone with a national reputation who in no way by the remotest suggestion can be accused of political influences as he administers that council.
Those are but one or two matters that I again bring to the Prime Minister's attention. We in this party are giving our support to the setting up of the council and to the principle of the bill. Over the years we have advocated the need for action along the lines suggested by the Massey commission. Frequently we have inquired as to when this council would be set up. It was only last June, as I recall it, that the Prime Minister gave as an explanation for delay the difficulty of securing the type of person requisite to the maintenance of the integrity and prestige of this council. What has taken place since then? Whom has the Prime Minister been in touch with? Who were those with whom he was in touch prior to June of last year when he felt impelled to explain, as the reason for the delay in setting up the council, that there were not available Canadians with the necessary ability for acceptance of positions on that council?
As I say, with the general principles of the bill we are in accord. We believe in the need for the extension of the humanities and the development of the things of the mind. We as Canadian citizens believe that a greater knowledge of our past achievements and of our history; the nourishing value of goodness; the lives of great men and women; the thoughts of those who changed the course of mankind; the experiences of recorded history; and the characters of literature and of works of art are of the essence of good citizenship. These things I believe will receive encouragement from the setting up of this council so that in the years ahead we in Canada may look back with pride on what is now being done and be able to give to the world renowned artists who will owe their opportunities for service in the arts to the patronage which will be given to them by the council and by the provision of assistance,

Canada Council
both by scholarship and by direct encouragement of the arts. However, in accepting the general principle of the bill and in giving it our support I say to the Prime Minister that we at the same time want to assure that the rights and privileges of parliament shall be maintained and that an organization set-up such as this shall, in the experience of Great Britain which has been found to be beneficial, require that parliament shall not by the simple expedient of passing legislation disavow its responsibility to assure that the expenditures made by the council shall be in the best interests of the Canadian people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that this matter received a thorough and wide discussion at the resolution stage and that it is therefore unnecessary to make any prolonged speeches on the second reading of the bill. However, I am rising to say that we are unanimous as a party in the support of this measure. We believe that this is something that is long overdue. A council of this description can do a great deal to assist in the development of Canada in a field other than that which we have been discussing for the last couple of days. We have been discussing the economic development of Canada, and now we have before us a bill which will assist in the development of Canada in the field of culture.
I am not forgetting that with the inadequate resources at the disposal of organizations across the country a great deal has been done already in the promotion of a distinctly Canadian culture. Sometimes when I listen to the people who have been brought into prominence on television and on the radio, when I see the fine productions that are made by Canadian artists, I am quite proud. Last Wednesday evening, I think it was, I saw a fine production on television of the story of Sir John A. Macdonald. I was greatly interested, greatly taken, and I am glad indeed to be able to say I should like to compliment the people who were responsible for that production. The same thing could be said of some of the other productions we have seen on television and heard over the radio from time to time, particularly on Wednesday evenings. I think the Wednesday evening program of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has done much to encourage the love of good music, the understanding of Canadian drama and to encourage young writers and artists in the development of their talents in these fields. I think that the Canada Council can do very much more along these lines.
Some years ago I suggested we might appropriate some money to be used for the purchase of pictures from Canadian artists
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
for the national gallery. I believe that, to some extent, that is being done today. It is true, we have purchased some other pictures that have been more costly, but they have added to the art treasures that Canada has collected over the years. I do not feel that parliament is wasting any money when it invests in that kind of cultural activity. I am pleased, too, to see that some arrangement is being made for scholarships and bursaries for the young men and women of Canada. We do not think enough is being done, even under this bill, or by any organizations in Canada to that end. However, to the extent we are doing something, I heartily welcome what is being done.
Of course, I agree that there should be a report made to parliament, and that we should be very careful with regard to the investments that are to be made. I am not going into the provisions of the bill because that would be improper but my reading of the bill is such that I think if the government of Canada appoints three of the five people who direct the investments that should give fairly complete control of the investments and ensure the people of Canada that these investments would not be made in stocks and other securities that might be subject to severe fluctuations and loss. If I know anything about the officials of the treasury department who, I imagine, would be obligated to do this kind of job or to give supervision to it, they would exercise every care. I am not gainsaying the argument that parliament should have the right to acquire knowledge of what is being done. A report is to be made to parliament 15 days after the session opens, but that might not be sufficient. However, one can go into that when we get into committee. But at least if the report is placed on the table of the house, it seems to me members would have the right to pick that report off the table and discuss it under one or the other of the opportunities we have for raising grievances or bringing before the house matters that require our attention.
I am not a bit nervous, of course, that this Canada Council is going to promote any subversive ideas across the country; quite the contrary. I am sure the people who will be appointed will be responsible people who can command the respect of this house and of the country. I think that to suggest this is going to be some sort of a cloak under which some strange ideas may infiltrate the culture of Canada is something that is not worth even discussing, indeed not worth mentioning. I am pleased indeed, on behalf of those associated with me, to give all the support we can to the second reading of this bill. I am hopeful that sooner or later satisfactory development will take place, and one day we

shall have in the capital cities of all the provinces-perhaps setting an example in this capital-cultural centres which will involve in Ottawa a national gallery and a national library. I look forward to the day when we may have a nationally subsidized auditorium or theatre in which we may be able to enjoy the best of Canadian talent in drama, music and art.
I want to say again that I am one of those who appreciate what is being done in some of the other places. Montreal, for instance, has become more or less a centre for certain types of music, opera and culture. I am glad to see that Toronto is doing the same thing. I am delighted with what is being done in Winnipeg in the realm of music, and what is being done in the city of Vancouver also. I hope that, sooner or later, the people of Canada will support expenditures which will give to this country a national theatre, and will incline them to subsidize opera, ballet and symphony orchestras. I want to add, if I may use a partial text from scripture, that man does not live by bread alone.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Since one week ago today, Mr. Speaker, when we last considered this measure we have heard nothing and seen nothing that would cause us to change our minds on this great question. We have read the bill and we find no solace in that.
First, I should like to say that we agree wholeheartedly with what the Leader of the Opposition has just said when he bemoans the fact that there is no opportunity for parliamentary supervision of this organization. We maintain that, considering the needs of this country on a priority basis, the time has not yet come for spending $100 million in this manner. As I said, there has been no reason advanced to cause us to change our thinking.
I am going to offer a suggestion right here, Mr. Speaker. Provided that the government is determined to spend this amount of money to promote culture rather than to provide a climate, as we maintain, in which culture can flourish and grow, we would ask the government to economize and forget setting up the council.
At the present time we have many organizations in this country that are doing a wonderful job in promoting culture throughout Canada. Some of them have been mentioned and I am not going to recall them at this time. But why not spend the $50 million in assistance to those very worthy and worthwhile organizations that are doing such a good job at the present time?
In my speech on February 6 I mentioned that we find it difficult to locate a definition
Canada Council
for the word "culture". An internationally-minded friend in New York wrote me a few days ago and provided me with an answer to my puzzle. The definition is provided in an anthology of Alfred North Whitehead published by Macmillan, New York, in 1953. Under the chapter, "The Aims of Education", you will find this definition of culture. I might mention that Mr. Whitehead is an English mathematician and a noted Harvard philosopher. This is his definition of culture:
Culture is activity of thought and receptiveness to beauty and humane feeling.
You will recall that during my few words of a week ago my whole argument was that one of the basic needs of this country was to provide a field in which culture could grow and flourish; in other words, to provide what this definition calls for, namely, receptiveness to beauty and humane feeling.
Then, I noticed in a paper published in New York, the New York Times, the heading "State of Culture Concerns Canada". A column was devoted to the debates on this question in the house. To a degree I would find fault with the heading, because those of us who are greatly concerned about this question of culture say that our concern is based on the fact that we see in this a method of promoting state culture. Therefore, we would agree with the heading 100 per cent if the word "of" were eliminated and the heading of the column became, "State Culture Concerns Canada". That is the phrase that is causing us great concern in this part of the house at the present time.
I believe I mentioned before the phrases that the Prime Minister used in explaining the possibilities as he saw them in this bill. He used the words "spiritual development" and the phrase "intellectual world brotherhood". Mr. Speaker, we are alarmed when we hear such words used as the aims of a national organization that is being set up to oversee the entire question of promoting culture in this country. I am sure that much opposition will develop in the minds of Canadians, especially Canadians with strong religious beliefs, and more especially of Canadians who are opposed to many of the state cultures that are rampant in the world today. I am sure that when this is publicized and brought home to some of the people in this country they will see an inherent danger in the promotion of a council whose aims are spiritual development and an intellectual world brotherhood. I am thinking of the people of Quebec, and the premier of that province who has steadfastly refused to accept grants from this government in aid of education. Those grants have amounted to millions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, and it may

Canada Council
not be amiss for me to say that I thought he was making a grave mistake. Possibly the premier of that province, though, is looking a little farther into the future than some of us are at the present time.

speechtext: He wants to keep our culture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Perhaps he sees in this policy that is now being developed the culmination of all his fears and the threat that he has felt may be attached to grants from the federal government. Therefore, he may be a smarter man than many of us have thought. Perhaps our criticism of his refusal to accept this money and to use it for educational purposes in his own province has been unfounded.
Then I recall that the Prime Minister attended a meeting in Quebec last summer. If I am wrong in this my excuse is that I am speaking from memory. I have a press clipping at home. As I recall it, our Prime Minister spoke in Quebec and dealt with the increasing demands for federal financial assistance. He propounded a theory along this line. The more financial assistance was demanded from the central government the more control would be exercised by the federal government over these matters to which financial assistance was given. In other words, we come back to the old adage, he who pays the piper calls the tune. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in these grants from the central authority, with the strings attached as provided in this bill, we see nothing but cause for alarm and cause for fear.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, we have consistently demanded that in all federal-provincial relations grants be given absolutely without strings, and we have not changed our opinion because of expediency.
As I said earlier, the provinces have many organizations. Our own province of British Columbia has an organization which is doing an excellent job# in promoting recreation commissions throughout the province. I am given to understand that in a very short time a new department will be set up under a minister of the crown which will have charge of the development of recreation and culture in the province of British Columbia. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there are many worthwhile organizations that could profitably use some of this $50 million that the central government is now providing, and they could use it more economically.
The council which is to be set up will cost money. We shall have salaried officials. There will be a permanent staff and there will be travelling expenses. Why the duplication? If we are really serious in this question of promoting culture why not make every dollar

possible available under the plan to the organizations which exist at the present time instead of duplicating the expenses and the services that are already provided in this country?
The various groups have cut short their remarks and I am going to do the same. However, I cannot let this opportunity pass without referring to a speech made by the hon. member for Nanaimo on February 6. It is not my habit, Mr. Speaker, to take a fellow member to task, if I may put it that way, or to criticize his efforts in this house. However, the hon. member made some remarks which I think are worthy of a moment's notice. I will say this, according to the definition of the word "culture", activity of thought, the hon. member is quite well imbued with that attribute. I believe that in his thinking he is placing the wrong construction upon much of the work that is done by the Social Credit group and many of the ideas that have been expressed in this house by members of that party. I am rather glad that he does this, Mr. Speaker, because I would be the first one to become a little suspicious if we in this group promoted any policy that received the full personal endorsement of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). He stated that we were "agin" sin.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago my leader said we were not going to delay the proceedings on second reading of this bill and I do not propose to do so. However, I would like to make reference to a statement which the Prime Minister made on January 18 when he was introducing the resolution for the establishment of the Canada Council. At that time the Prime Minister paid tribute to the courageous venture at Stratford, Ontario. He was, of course, referring to the Stratford Shakespearean festival. As this venture has undoubtedly been the greatest achievement of its kind on the North American continent, I feel I should mention briefly some of its accomplishments.
This undertaking originated in the mind of a Stratford man, Tom Patterson, who is now internationally known in this field. From that seed of imagination and through the untiring efforts of successive boards of governors and the contributions of individuals and business the Stratford festival has grown in stature to the point where it takes second place to no similar project in the world.
The first performance in 1953 took place under canvas. Today a new permanent theatre is being constructed at a cost of
Canada Council
$1,500,000. This new theatre will be completed in time to house the 1957 plays. I know I am prejudiced and I presume others will agree that I am but at the same time it occurs to me that this is the type of venture to which the Canada Council might well consider giving some assistance in the future. I would like to take a few moments to indicate just what the combined efforts in Stratford really accomplished during 1956 as a consequence of which I am led to believe that the Canada Council can contribute much to the welfare of Canada and to our national unity. I would impress upon the house that one of the main objectives of the festival is that it aspires to be a national enterprise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that I hope my words will indicate that the establishment of the Canada Council will be of some benefit to all of Canada and will make a valid contribution to national unity. I really mean what I have said and I do not know what more I can say. I would like to continue my remarks very briefly. I feel that I am on the right track and that my comments relate to the principle of the bill. Certain clauses of the bill do refer to the theatre and to assistance to the theatre. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will illustrate just what I mean.
One of the main objectives of the festival is that it aspires to be a national enterprise. In 1956 that objective was accomplished. As we know there are two great cultures in Canada, one rooted in the English tongue and one in the French tongue. Of course other cultures do exist in this country but not in such strength. One of the plays produced at Stratford in 1956 was Henry V. In this play there are many French-speaking characters. The Stratford company received an invitation to perform at the Edinburgh festival in Scotland and partly for the sake of the play but also to make the company more representative than hitherto of all Canada the Frenchspeaking characters in the play were cast with French Canadian actors. As a result of this casting the English-French conflict of the play was developed with perhaps more

Canada Council
meaning than ever before. Canada is probably the only country in the world that could stage such an interpretation of Henry V.
This undertaking was a considerable gamble and the French Canadian actors were required to portray difficult parts in English.
I might point out that failure of the play would have harmed the reputation of French Canadian actors more than the Stratford foundation. The actors went to great pains to master, appreciate and enjoy the different language in its Shakespearean form. Their courage, hard work and artistry won the deep respect and admiration not only of the Canadian and United States press but also, and perhaps this is of more importance, the respect and admiration of their fellow English-speaking artists.
These artists from Quebec were also invited by the foundation to provide Englishspeaking Canadians with a taste of French culture during the festival last year by performing in French the three Moliere farces with which they had been so successful in Paris the previous summer. I am convinced it was not dollars that attracted these French-Canadian artists to Stratford last summer. They could have found more lucrative jobs in television studios in Montreal than the Stratford festival could afford. I am sure they admired what had been achieved by English-speaking Canadians in Stratford. I am also convinced that they considered the whole project a challenge.
Probably the acceptance of this challenge by the French-Canadian artists was more especially due to the fact that they realized, as did the Stratford foundation, the dangers of some of the prejudices which exist between English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians. They realized further that in a world which is struggling for amicable understanding between nations, if within one of the nations concerned there are two groups unwilling to respect and learn from each other's differences of character, taste and culture, there can be little hope for a wider understanding being created on an international scale.
Any hindrance to a mutual understanding between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians seems to these artists and to the Stratford foundation to deny to the inhabitants of Canada one of her greatest nonmaterial riches. Art is an international rather than a national affair, and it is mainly through the interchange of cultural expressions that one country can come to understand and appreciate another. If, through a modest example of such artistic interchange, some of the unhappy prejudices existing between different parts of Canada can be exposed for

what they are really worth, a definite contribution has been made to national unity.
Mr. Speaker, I have talked to many of these artists from Montreal's Theatre du Nouveau Monde and I have talked to many of the English-speaking actors and actresses.
I have also discussed the whole venture with the producer of Henry Y, Mr. Michael Lang-ham. In fact it was Mr. Langham who drove home to me just how much this mingling of the two cultures has meant and could mean to a more clear understanding of each other.
I believe last summer's experiment in Stratford has served to create a health invigorating stimulus to Canada's maturing character.
I believe the formation of a Canada Council, Mr. Speaker, will further any original progress in this respect made last year in Stratford.
Might I say a word about an organization which has developed in Stratford subsequent to the success of the festival? This organization, known as "Canadian Players", is now for the third year touring Canada and the United States, employing, practically, 100 per cent professional Canadian artists. Employment is being provided for these people for several months of the year. A very important point is that they have provided enjoyment for thousands of people in remote parts of nine provinces of Canada.
There are, I think, several important questions to be asked when we are dealing with the various sections of the bill, but within the over-all picture I do believe the existence of a Canada Council will result in more of our people enjoying the various arts.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier that the new permanent theatre in Stratford will be opened to house this year's Shakespearean festival. The traditional ceremony of laying the corner stone was performed by His Excellency the Governor General some two and a half weeks ago. It is proposed to continue the national character of the productions.
As any election will, no doubt, be over by the opening date of the Stratford festival 1957 season, I would certainly suggest to the house that attendance at the plays would be a very desirable method of relaxing after a strenuous campaign. And, of course, the excellent entertainment would drive away any disconsolate thoughts in the minds of those of us who may not be returning to the house.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) introduced this legislation some days ago I found there were a good many things he said with which I agreed wholeheartedly. I certainly have no quarrel with

the statement that there is a part which the federal government can play in the cultural field, and 1 cannot find any quarrel with the idea of awarding scholarships or with the idea of public funds being devoted to the assistance of culture or of grants being made to the universities.
As far as grants to universities are concerned, I think everyone in this house knows that we have always supported assistance of this sort being given. We have supported increases in the amount of these grants; as a matter of fact during this present session we supported the doubling of grants to universities. So, with regard to all these suggestions, we have no quarrel whatsoever.
There are, nevertheless, a few questions which do concern us with regard to the Canada Council. Many of them, possibly all of them, have been mentioned before by members of this group. The first question is: Is there a need for this Canada Council? The leader of this group some time ago questioned whether or not we did need the Canada Council, bearing in mind, among other things, the initial expense that would be involved in setting up the organization, paying its staff and so on. We already have here in Canada cultural groups which, with a little financial assistance from the government, could carry on any of the duties which would be performed by the Canada Council. We have also the cultural branches set up by the various provincial governments. I do not know what the names of these branches are in all the different provinces, but in the province of Alberta the department which deals with this is called the cultural branch and is looked after by the minister of economic affairs. These branches concern themselves with the cultural needs and requirements of the various provinces, and I think they do so very adequately. We have a Canadian conference of universities which certainly knows the needs of the universities as far as grants and scholarships are concerned.
All the proposals which have been advocated could certainly be accomplished by the work of these groups, or a combination of these groups, grants being made available to these organizations and scholarships given to the universities. It could be done without any centralization whatsoever, and done as well as and possibly better than it would be under the scheme now proposed.
Another point which has worried me is whether or not there is to be a clearly recognized priority with regard to scholarships and a recognized priority of art patronage. What guarantee would we have that "handouts" would not go to well-organized pressure

As far as the scholarship angle is concerned, in my opinion one of the first things that should have consideration is the field of science, and that should come before scholarships are meted out for the advancement of the arts. Many times during various debates in the house-and we have seen many reports on the matter in the press of the country-we have heard about the tremendous shortage of skilled workers, engineers, etc. Comparisons have been given as to the number of engineers being graduated behind the iron curtain and the number being graduated in the western democratic countries. Certainly if there is a shortage of such persons they are the first who should have access to any scholarships that are being handed out.
At the present time the western nations are involved in a production race against the forces of world communism, and if the reports we have received and the comparisons we have seen are true we are being out-produced because of our failure to graduate sufficient skilled workers to keep abreast. If that is so, the first thing we should do is see that people of this type are given an education

Canada Council
in order to protect our very existence as a democratic country, and then give scholarships for the arts once we have assured ourselves that we are going to be able to compete and exist in this world.
I should also like to know what guarantee there will be that the council, if it is politically loaded, will not be able to circumvent parliament. It was said the other day that if it appeared to be necessary a nominal amount could be put in the estimates in order to allow parliament to discuss the Canada Council. I suggest that there be an amount right from the first year. It does not matter what it is. It can be the traditional one dollar, but at least that would give us an opportunity to wage a full-scale debate concerning the affairs of the Canada Council at every session of parliament.
Another thing that has been bothering me is the personnel of the council. What qualifications will be sought and required in the appointment of the members of the council? I ask the Prime Minister whether he can give the house the assurance that the government in making these appointments will steer clear of former cabinet ministers and others closely and actively associated with politics. As one of the leading Liberal newspapers in Alberta has put it, stay clear of the culture vultures. In that regard can we be given the assurance that the council will not become a haven for retired and tired politicians, or a means of repaying political favours? If appointments are going to be made on a political basis, then this thing can become the sweetest pork barrel the country has known in quite a long time.

Surely we cannot legislate a true Canadian culture and foist it on the Canadian people. I am always a little bit suspicious of a state culture. It smacks of what they have in Russia and it could easily be used-I am not saying it will be used but that it could easily be used-to slant people's minds in almost any direction when the policy is put into the hands of a small group of people who are apparently to determine who is going to formulate the culture.
Rather than all these things I would say this to the government. When you bear in mind the fact that the people themselves are the ones who bring forth the culture, the proper thing for the government to do would be to institute fiscal and financial policies which would make it possible for Canadians to afford to go to those cultural centres that are now in existence. Mr. Speaker, I should not like this debate to close without saying a brief word. I recognize the dangers which have been outlined by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I recognize that there is a danger of trying to slant views, and that eventually the time may come when I may be accusing the Canada Council of trying to do that. But at the moment it seems to me that the matter is very simple, and I should like in a word to say why I shall vote for this bill.
It is inevitable that in this house we spend nearly all our time dealing with what I shall call the means of life. I refer to wheat; coal; money, much money, much money as the versifier of the Globe and Mail said; uranium, and all the other things we know about. That is what we are obliged to spend our time on, and it is essential that we do so. What I like about this bill is that for a moment we are addressing our minds to what seem to me to be the ends of life-I refer to beauty and truth-and we are trying to do our best to assist the things which promote them, such as good literature, painting, good music and drama, all the things that we know in our hearts are much more important than are the things upon which we are forced to spend our time day by day.
It is for that reason that I shall vote for this bill. In spite of all the difficulties that exist I hope it may do a great deal to promote those things which after all lie behind the things we deal with from day to day.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I thought I tried to make clear, I had no intention of discussing this unmentionable branch as such; but I was about to say that I had come to the conclusion, from the manner in which the hon. member for Wetaskiwin had judged the approach that he felt the government was making in setting up a Canada Council, that it could only have arisen out of his experience with the manner

in which that particular cultural branch was used by the government of the province from which he comes.
If one were to judge from the discussion, Mr. Speaker, one would think this bill was going to set up some super organization that would rule the thinking and cultural activities of the Canadian people with an iron hand. I think there might be some point in reminding the house at this stage of the description that is given of the purpose of this bill in the explanatory note. After reading the bill clause by clause it seems to me that note sets forth the purpose of the bill fairly well. The explanatory note reads:
The purpose of this bill is to authorize the establishment of a Canada Council for the encouragement of the arts, humanities and social sciences in Canada. For this purpose the council will assist, co-operate with and enlist the aid of organizations the objects of which are similar to any of the objects of the council.
Perhaps it might be well to interject that, as I understand it, the fact that the government has seen fit to take action by introducing this bill has resulted largely from the representations that have been made from time to time by some of the organizations referred to in the explanatory note which, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin suggested, are engaged in various activities along the lines the council will seek to follow. The explanatory note goes on:
The work of the council will be financed from the earnings of an endowment fund to be established by this bill. In assisting Canadian universities in their building construction projects, however, the council will be authorized, after certain conditions have been met, to use a second sum of money to be known as the university capital grants fund.
Provision is also made for the council to receive, expend and administer any gifts and bequests that may be made to it.
Possibly the reading of that explanatory note may be repetitious in the over-all debate, but I have read it because I think it does, by its very wording, bring into some reasonable perspective some of the outlandish claims to which we have just been listening in respect of the things the council will do and will not do. Do not expect to see, as a result of the passage of this bill, any great change in the cultural life or activities of Canadian people overnight. But I think the basic purpose which is set forth shows that it is designed to foster growth, which must -and here I agree with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin-come from the lives of the individual people. It is something which we can and should support. The suggestion that because this bill happens to be introduced in the federal parliament of Canada rather than under the auspices of one of our provincial governments that makes it any more a state venture is, on the face of it, absurd.

If the hon. member for Peace River was not there referring to the Canada Council I would suggest he might, on some occasion, get up and explain to what he was referring.
I have been giving a little thought to how our life in this country is enriched in the field of the arts, the social sciences and the humanities. Perhaps because of the fact that certain remarks such as "canned culture" have been made by one of the members representing an Alberta constituency I have cast my mind back to the situation that prevailed when my mother came with her parents to what is now central Alberta, somewhere around the year 1889. I have been wondering whether because my grandfather saw fit to bring with him a few boxes of books so he might give something beyond the daily toil of farming to his children who were growing up, he was thereby importing canned culture into Canada.
I have wondered, too, whether when my grandfather and some of his neighbours got together and organized a form of government which built those little square frame school houses out there in the middle of the farming country, because of the fact that they had taken what amounted to governmental action to provide the opportunity for the children to go to school and acquire a little more than what they might learn by milking cows, they were introducing canned culture into Canada. I have also wondered whether because of the fact that certain government agencies took the steps that were necessary to provide a normal school in the

Canada Council
city of Regina to which my mother might go to train to be a teacher, we were getting closer to complete control by canned culture in Canada.
When the citizens of the province of Alberta in due course got around to establishing an institution on the banks of the North Saskatchewan river, which is known as the University of Alberta, were they by that action introducing canned culture into Canada? You know, it is quite surprising to me to hear anybody who comes from western Canada, where almost everything we have in the way of opportunities of learning anything more than the things that were required to make a living, has been the result of initiative taken by governments, oppose a measure of this kind.
When the government of the province of British Columbia went to the point of expanding a college, which had sprung out of McGill University, into a state university in that province, was it by that action introducing canned culture into the province of British Columbia? And so it goes. Let us keep this thing in perspective. Let us recognize that anything in the field of the social sciences, the humanities or the arts comes as a result of knowledge and experience gained by individual human beings, and all that any collective agency can do is to foster it.
That is the purpose set out in this bill, to encourage, to assist, to co-operate with, to enlist the aid of. If this bill purported to do anything more than that, then I would agree it would be something that might be of questionable value. Of course, those of us who are prepared to support the bill recognize that its value will depend largely upon the use made of it; but let us not attempt to trample it into the dust before it has had a chance to show its first bud.
There is a certain disposition in some quarters, Mr. Speaker, to think that culture is for the millionaires or for the sons of millionaires, and for that reason I should like to put on the record what the Canadian Labour Congress had to say about the Canada Council in its memorandum to the government on January 23, 1957:
We wish to commend the Prime Minister on his announcement that parliament will be asked to approve the creation of the Canada Council. We believe that such encouragement in the field of arts and letters is long overdue. The Canadian Labour Congress would like to remind the government that within the affiliated membership of the congress there are many who will be directly affected by the activities of the Canada Council. We suggest that representation from these areas of the population be considered when the members of the council are named.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while we are on this point may I say I certainly hope that the

recommendations of the Canadian Labour Congress in this connection will be given due consideration because, as I sense the feeling of the working people of Canada today, more and more they are coming to realize that, if not for themselves, as least for their sons and daughters they want much greater opportunities in the fields that will be supported by the Canada Council than they have had heretofore.
I must say that in reading the brief submission on the subject of the Canada Council from the Canadian Labour Congress I am proud that I am a member of one of the constituent organizations of that congress, and that I can stand up here in parliament with considerable confidence, in the knowledge that as far as the responsible members of my trade union organization are concerned we will back this Canada Council idea right down the line, and do everything we can to assist and foster it into a long and useful life in Canada.
The intentions along that line are becoming more and more apparent all the time. It is only within the last week or two that I saw a report of a certain trade union institute which was held on Vancouver island, in one of the centres of my own constituency. Trade union representatives came to that institute from quite a wide area. One of the people with whom they had discussion and to whom they listened was one of the professors of the University of British Columbia. This question of support for the area of activity which it is envisaged the Canada Council will foster was to the fore in that discussion.
I also noticed in the last issue of the B.C. Lumber Worker two or three full pages of pictures devoted to a visit by one of the members of my local union to the University of British Columbia, which his two sons are attending, and the tour that was made in connection with the plea that is being put forward by the students for more accommodation at the university. The reason that was given that sort of play in the B. C. Lumber Worker was that the people who work in the logging camps, in the sawmills and in the plywood plants in British Columbia know they want something more than the jobs from which they earn their daily bread, not only for themselves but for their sons and daughters. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should not pay too much attention to the dire forebodings we have been hearing from some of the members of the Social Credit group. If they have those fears let them keep an eagle eye on the activities of the council, and if they can find legitimate grounds for criticism of its activities by all means let them sound forth with them.

Mr. Speaker, when I rose in this house on January 15, to take part in the debate on the address, here is what I said:
In regard to university grants, I shall have the privilege of discussing them when the bill is before us.
We have now reached the second reading of the bill submitted by the Prime Minister himself (Mr. St. Laurent), whereby we were asked to approve grants amounting to $50 million to assist Canadian universities.
All members in this house without exception, whatever their political affiliation, recognize the precarious financial situation of our institutions of higher learning and know how great are the needs of our universities. The creation of new faculties is necessary, indeed it is essential, in this modern world in which we live and in which science, in all its aspects, plays a leading part. For that, new buildings must be erected and equipped at a cost of millions of dollars; teachers are increasing in numbers all the time and their ability, in their respective fields, must be reasonably rewarded. It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that if our universities had waited for assistance from the federal government to do their job, to diffuse science and to educate our youth, our country would surely not be at the intellectual level that can be pridefully credited to it today.
Other organizations, since confederation, have looked after that problem of higher education, and their work in that field can really be called sublime. All our admiration should go to those who have in turn run universities and who have made almost heroical sacrifices.
On the other hand, the provinces have, since 1867, in spite of low budgets and pressure from all sides by countless requests due to the rapid development of a modern world, constantly earmarked large amounts for primary and higher education.
In this way, they fulfilled an obligation conferred upon them by the Canadian constitution, which placed education at every level under exclusive provincial jurisdiction and gave the provinces the sole right to levy taxes to this effect.
Canada Council
The province of Quebec has always jealously preserved the exclusive right to legislate on educational matters, and in spite of numerous and repeated attempts by the federal government to intervene in this field, its position has remained unaltered to this day.
The present head of the Quebec government, and those who work with him, are not the first to oppose federal encroachment in the academic field. Their opposition is therefore nothing new. The present government in my province vigorously follows a noble tradition initiated by its predecessors and ever since observed. All the former governments, Liberal and Conservative, and more particularly those headed by men like Gouin, Mercier and Taschereau, have led a fierce battle against any attempts by Ottawa at centralization in the educational field.
The leaders of yesterday, as well as today, saw and still look upon federalism as conceived by the fathers of confederation- according to the expression used by the chief editor of the Quebec Action Catholique, Dr. Louis-Philippe Roy, "... as the only one to offer sufficient guarantees to the French ethnical element, with its culture, its language, its way of life and its most cherished institutions."
Why has the Prime Minister of Canada abandoned such well-established tradition initiated by the great Liberal leaders of his province, if not to satisfy the greed of those who, like himself, are promoting a dangerous centralization in the hands of a single authority.
The Prime Minister can in no way deny that education in all its forms is the exclusive responsibility of the provincial legislatures, according to the terms of the constitution. The fathers of confederation knew in 1867 that Quebec was to become the heart and soul of French Canada and that, such being the case, the control of our education had to be left to the sole jurisdiction of the government of our province.
It must not be forgotten that if, prior to 1867, there had been no French Canada, this precious and indispensable document we call the Canadian constitution would never have been written. In other words, if there had not been French-speaking Canadians in Canada in 1867, with a religion differing from that of the majority, with a culture of their own and a way of life that was not that of other Canadians, there would have been no confederation. In brief, had it not been for this duality of culture, language, religion and customs, we would now be living in a legislative union and not in a confederation.
And if at that moment the province of Quebec, then called Lower Canada, had been

Canada Council
refused guarantees according to which education would be exclusively reserved to it our illustrious French-speaking ancestors would have categorically rejected the Canadian confederation.
It must then be recognized that 90 years ago it was admitted that the province of Quebec would not be just one province among others. That explains the step taken at the time to protect its peculiar character and ensure its survival. The fathers of confederation desired Canada to possess two distinct cultures, those that make our country what it has become today. That is why they took the action necessary to preserve these cultures and guarantee their survival.
When the Prime Minister of Canada suggests to universities of the province of Quebec that they accept money from the federal government without paying any attention to the opposition of the provincial authorities I say that he is setting a very bad example for all his fellow citizens. Not only does his behaviour come as a challenge to a democratically established provincial authority, but such an attitude constitutes a new and flagrant violation of the Canadian constitution. The Prime Minister should stop talking to us about his favourite topic, Canadian unity, because his repeated assaults against the constitution have largely contributed to the setting up of disagreements in this country and to rousing the rest of Canada against the province of Quebec.
His repeated attacks against Quebec are designed to lead those who live outside of my province into believing that its leaders are not doing their duty in the field of education, and more particularly, perhaps, as far as university education is concerned.
Therefore I deem it my duty to tell the Canadian people today that the province of Quebec has done more for education, in proportion to her population, than any other province of confederation. Again this year, the Quebec provincial legislature has provided an appropriation of $106,812,000 for all levels and all forms of education. It is worth pointing out that the huge amount of $13,153,700 is provided for assistance to Quebec universities; that is an increase of $5,063,133 over the previous fiscal year. Thus my province has earmarked for education 22.6 per cent of her budget; all reasonable Canadians will admit that this high percentage is unprecedented in our history.
How can the federal government, on the eve of a general election, decide to offer this year $50 million to the Canadian universities, thus invading a field where it has no jurisdiction?
It is because it takes in revenue which does not belong to it, which it retains in

spite of its wartime promises and which it wishes to retain at all costs in spite of the energetic protests of those who still respect the Canadian constitution.

The Liberal government will try to make voters believe that it is distributing those gifts out of its own revenue, whereas the people of this country know full well that those grants to universities as well as the hundreds of millions of dollars paid out in family allowances, old age pensions, pensions to the blind and disabled are financed by funds which have been taken from the provinces and are being used today to delude the people in order that the Liberals may remain in power.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of denying the other provinces the right to accept federal grants for their universities. Their position is different from that of Quebec. The autonomy of these other provinces is no less in jeopardy but federal interference in their educational responsibilities is not attended by such serious consequences. As for us, in Quebec, we must preserve our culture and we will do so in spite of the repeated attacks of the centralizers who insult us by pretending to believe that our province stands in the way of progress of Canada and of national unity.
Should we remove from our country this duality of cultures which is so characteristic of it, should we attempt to assimilate or destroy one of them, we would find that we destroyed the glory of our ancestors and the pride of our history.
How can we settle the disagreement between Quebec and Ottawa which creates so much confusion in the minds of people? How are we to face that problem and how are we to solve it? How are we to allow Quebec to satisfy the immense needs of our universities without infringement upon our autonomy in the field of education, an autonomy of which we are rightly so mindful? The answer is quite simple. Let the federal government put an end to its centralizing ambitions, let it put an end to its invasion of the taxation fields reserved to the provinces, let it cease

collecting direct taxes for provincial purposes which are the exclusive field of the provinces. In brief, let it respect fully the Canadian constitution.
It is imperative that there be a new federal-provincial conference in the shortest possible delay, that is to say before the dissolution of this parliament, in order to determine once and for all the taxation powers of the federal and provincial governments. As long as the central power invades the taxation fields which are exclusively reserved to the provinces for provincial purposes, such as education and many other fields, it can expect stubborn resistance from all those who claim no special privilege but demand respect for their rights.
What the federal government is doing now is wrong; it is creating a dangerous precedent, which will have serious repercussions.
If ever Canada falls under a Socialist government, what will happen to French culture in our country? These proponents of centralization would soon crush our constitution, as the Liberals are doing today, and would standardize Canadian culture. We must prevent that danger and it is our duty in Quebec to fight by all constitutional means at our disposal the invasion of the field of education by the central power. He who pays the piper calls the tune. The French minority rightly fears that this is what will happen in the future.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion may I say that it is highly regrettable to find that the man who, more than any other, has encroached upon the Canadian constitution and has thus helped most to reduce the influence which should be exercised by French-speaking Canadians is himself a French-speaking Prime Minister coming from the province of Quebec. His actions and his attitude, ever since he has been at the head of the government, have been in complete contradiction with his words. The Prime Minister of Canada could certainly never boast of having promoted unity. His greatest contribution will have been to national disunity.

During the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, I think we have seen a good deal of fancy footwork on the part of hon. members to our left. We have had speeches in which they protest very vehemently that they are in favour of culture, and then in the next breath they do a great disservice to the cause of the Canada Council. In the last remarks made by the hon. member for Macleod just before he resumed his seat I think he made the statement that they are not in favour of anything which would mould the thinking of Canadians into one mind. I think a statement like that in itself indicates a lack of appreciation of what is meant by the Canada Council.
I have read the report of the Massey commission over very carefully, and I am satisfied that the Canada Council which is being set up is in line with the recommendations of that commission. I have a great deal of respect for the personnel of that commission. I had the opportunity of sitting in on some of the hearings in the city of Saskatoon while I was attending the University of Saskatchewan. I feel that the recommendations of that commission which led to the introduction of this legislation give the lie to any of the suggestions that have been raised by those who are in outright opposition to the setting up of the council.
The royal commission states that there are in Canada many voluntary organizations whose work is of national importance. It goes on to point out that there does not exist in Canada any board or council to advise the government in this matter. If we are going to give any assistance to the arts, I prefer to see that assistance given through a body such as the Canada Council rather than through the government itself. I asked the hon. member for Wetaskiwin an hour ago whether he would prefer that the government be called upon to make grants to the various cultural organizations in Canada rather than having those grants made part of an over-all policy directed by a body such as the Canada Council, which I presume will have representation from various parts of Canada. In line with the recommendation made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I would certainly impress upon the government the necessity of appointing as a member of the council a representative of the Canadian Labour Congress.
I was rather perturbed at some of the remarks made this afternoon, particularly

Canada Council
those to the effect that we have in Canada today certain voluntary organizations which are well able to carry on this work. As is well known to all members of this house, those voluntary organizations referred to are indeed carrying on extremely important work in this country. But I think we will also agree that they are starved for funds. I noted a press report the other day to the effect that the Stratford festival was approaching the federal government with a request for some financial assistance to enable it to complete the capital construction of a theatre in the city of Stratford so the festival might be carried on as the closest thing to a national theatre that we have in Canada.
We know the story about the dominion drama festival. Apparently it found it very difficult to carry on, and this has been made possible only through the contributions made by a distillery in this country. I do not know whether or not my hon. friends to the left would prefer to have these voluntary organizations going around begging for funds and depending upon distilleries in order to carry on their operations. I would think the Canadian people would much rather provide for those things themselves through their government and through a body such as the Canada Council.
The same could be said about travelling art exhibitions. A couple of years ago I went to the fair in Regina and noticed a lot of young people coming out of a building carrying booklets of reproductions of fine paintings of Canadian cities. I noticed also very prominently displayed on the covers of those booklets the name of a very well known Canadian distillery. It seems to me these organizations about which my hon. friends to the left have been very much concerned are the very organizations that have been asking for the Canada Council. They are the very organizations that have been asking the government for some form of assistance.
I suggest it is not the concern for these voluntary organizations expressed by the Social Credit group that brings them into opposition to the measure now before the house. While they claim in the speeches they have given that they are in favour of culture, they have done everything within their power to sow the seeds of suspicion and discord, and make the task of the Canada Council much more difficult.
This afternoon there were insinuations about state culture. I think Russia was mentioned. This has been an attempt to smear the Canada Council before it is set up. It seems to me you cannot prejudge a body of this kind. I am certain that we in
[Mr. Ellis.1
this group are going to be very watchful of the activities of the Canada Council, and if the council is not doing the type of work which I am sure all hon. members who have read the Massey report believe it should be undertaking, then we will have something to say at that time. We are certainly not going to prejudge the Canada Council and oppose it simply because of some vague fears which have never materialized in the United Kingdom, or in any part of the free world in which a body such as this has been established.
There have been a number of references, and there was a little skirmish a while ago, on this question of canned culture. I believe the Canada Council will be one of the most effective means of combating canned culture. I envisage it as a body which will encourage the development of Canadian talent. I want to see Canadian actors on Canadian stages. I want to hear an allCanadian symphony orchestra. I want to see a truly national ballet. These are the things to which a Canada Council can lead. This is not canned culture, it is the reverse of it. I suggest that expressions like "canned culture" are the worst expressions which could be used by anyone who pretends to be interested in the development of the arts in this country.
It seems to me that these voluntary bodies that are going to be incorporated into the structure of the Canada Council are going to be able to do a more effective job through the creation of the council itself, because it is a body which has been needed for a long time. Yet we find the rather ridiculous situation of people who oppose the Canada Council out of hand pretending to be concerned about the voluntary bodies, when these same voluntary bodies are the ones who have been promoting the Canada Council. In my view it is not the government that is pushing the Canada Council, it is the voluntary organizations who have been pushing the government. It is these bodies who have been persistent in getting the government to follow the recommendations of the Massey commission with respect to the Canada Council.
I suggest that the reason this has been the case is that they realize that is the best method of granting assistance, through a body under which there can be some coordination. I do not know what other means could be used. I understand there are a few bodies in Canada that have been receiving some small grants from the government and, as the Massey commission suggests, that is not a good practice.
I would say that I would much prefer to see any grants made by a government

handled by an all-inclusive representative body such as the Canada Council because, oddly enough, I think the government would be far more prone to take into account political considerations than any body such as the Canada Council.
