Any interpretation or implication can be made in the house or out of the house from what has been said by the Social Credit members, but the facts remain and our position has been clearly stated throughout the debate on this bill. The things that have been said and the implications that have been taken from what has been said do not alter the facts; the facts remain.
I am opposed to this Canada Council being set up at this time. I would have you note that this is the tone we have taken throughout the debate, and the record shows that we are against the setting up of the Canada Council at this time. There are a number of reasons why we are opposed to it being set up at this time. I do not believe the people generally across this country understand fully what the council is or what it pretends to be. I am sure the people are not aware of the amount of money that is involved in this bill. I do not believe the Massey report envisaged a large amount of money such as $100 million dropped in in one splash.
We feel we represent the views of the people when our leader mentioned that there should be priorities. Now, "priority" means there is something that is going to take place before something else takes place, so this 82715-81J
Canada Council
does not preclude the establishment at some time of a Canada Council.
I was interested in some statements concerning this bill that were recorded in Hansard during the resolution stage. I should like to comment just briefly on one or two of them.
The Prime Minister said, on January 18, as found at page 392 of Hansard:
In Canada our spiritual growth must naturally be drawn from the traditional cultures of the two peoples that mainly make up the Canadian nation and from the cultures that many other groups have brought to us.
Personally I do not believe the Prime Minister meant just that. As a matter of fact it is my belief-and he can correct me if I am wrong-that he meant exactly the reverse of what he said. It is my belief that culture is drawn from the spiritual experiences of man and his relation to those things which are natural, rather than vice versa. I may be wrong, but I certainly believe that it is out of the heart of man and his spiritual experiences that real culture develops.
At page 396 of Hansard the Prime Minister quoted a resolution adopted by the university representatives at their meeting last fall, as follows:
Their considered opinion that it was their urgent duty to warn the people of Canada that the problem of universities has become an emergency of national concern to the certain disadvantage of our progress and standing as a nation, and can only be solved by the energetic and immediate assistance and co-operation of all governments in Canada, of business and industry and of private benefactors.
In commenting on this resolution the Prime Minister had this to say:
It seems to me that the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament should not ignore such a serious warning and should be prepared to make a contribution, which can be made through the Canada Council to meet this emergency.
It is my feeling, Mr. Speaker, that while what the Prime Minister said is correct, the Canada Council does not meet the need that is envisioned in his statement. It is my understanding that the $50 million is for capital expenditure for the purpose of making more people aware of the work being done in the arts, humanities and social sciences. If that is true, then it is an addition to what we already have and not a help to meet the need that is expressed in the quotation I have just read.
I should like to make one other comment on what the Prime Minister had to say on pages 977 and 988 of Hansard of February 5. I do not think I need to read the quotation on the last page I mentioned, as the second

Canada Council
quotation is an enlargement of the first. The first quotation reads:
It was for the purpose of creating this hody in such a way that it would not be subject to frequent pressures in the allocation of the funds which would be placed at its disposal.
The Prime Minister enlarged on that by saying that this government, or any other government to follow, should not be in a position to say:
Well, now, this is the situation. You get nothing unless our views are met.
It is my feeling that this is a reflection on "the Canadian voters who return a government, whether it be a Liberal government, a Conservative government, a C.C.F. government or a Social Credit government. I may be wrong in that, and if so the Prime Minister can correct me when he speaks.
I wish to say one other thing, and then I shall finish. I should like to quote from Hansard at page 1009, where the Prime Minister said:
But it was felt it would be a good, proper stimulus to provide an initial endowment fund amounting to as much as $100 million and created at the expense of the whole Canadian public.
I do feel that the Prime Minister tried to soften that statement when he mentioned the two windfalls, and tried to leave the impression with the country that this extra money was not taxpayers' money although it came in large amounts. I do not think we should differentiate between the small amount that comes from the small taxpayer and the large amount that comes from the large taxpayer. I was also interested to note what the Leader of the Opposition said in respect of the fathers of confederation leaving the business of education to the provinces. I believe he should have followed along that same line of thinking a little farther than he did.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes to deal with one specific phase of this legislation. So far, as the Prime Minister mentioned, there has been very general approval of the legislation before us this afternoon with the exception of one party. I shall not enter into the controversy concerning the attitude taken by my Social Credit friends, which has been dealt with by other members in this group, except to say that I am disturbed by their attitude.
I am not disturbed because they are opposing this bill because that is their right and privilege, and they may have some reasons for opposing it other than those stated so far. I was disturbed, however, and I think many Canadians will be disturbed, by the attitude they have adopted in attempting to arouse a suspicion and in attempting to make this bill appear as something sinister which in my opinion it is not. I am also disturbed at their attempt to inject political motives into a body which if it is going to be effective should be above partisan considerations.
My purpose in rising is simply to place before the Prime Minister a request which I think is urgent, and it relates to the way in which the Canada Council and its activities will bear upon what are known as the ethnic groups in Canada. The term "ethnic groups" is I think now well known, and refers to those language groups other than English and French which are the two main language groups in Canada.
Yesterday a group called the Canadian ethnic press club visited Ottawa and presented a statement to the minister and his colleagues. I had the opportunity along with my leader to meet this body and address them, as I am sure many hon. members did. In their submission they set out certain recommendations in connection with what they term the integration of new Canadians into our Canadian way of life.
In that same connection I find that on February 6 of this year a statement was made to the Prime Minister by the Ukrainian Canadian committee, which represents a large body of people in this country. I would like to place on the record one or two paragraphs from that statement, because I think it sets out clearly the attitude taken by this ethnic group and I believe it accurately describes the attitude of all ethnic groups in Canada. In their letter to the Prime Minister of February 6, after commenting on his speech of January 10 when he introduced the resolution, the Ukrainian Canadian committee said: The Ukrainian Canadian committee representing all Ukrainian democratic organizations, heartily supports that resolution, in which we see an earnest effort to assure a brilliant future for the cultural development of Canada. We' recognize that even
Canada Council
the greatest material resources that our country is endowed with, cannot adequately fulfil the great mission of Canada, if we do not provide for the development of the spiritual and cultural values of the Canadian people. Individuals and nations are principally spiritual beings and shallow indeed are those countries in which there is no spiritual food for their citizens.
I place that on the record because I think it is an excellent way to illustrate the attitude taken by this particular group, and in this instance I think it speaks in the true voice of all ethnic groups in Canada. I am skipping parts of the letter in the interests of saving time, but it proceeds to request that the Ukrainian Canadians be represented on the Canada Council. I think I should place their request on the record in their own words. The paragraph setting out the request reads as follows:
The Ukrainian Canadians fully realize the fact that there are two principal cultures in this country. We recognize, however, that there is also a large, though miscellaneous third element that is not represented by these cultures. It is logical, therefore, that Ukrainians, with their colourful cultural heritage, should seek representation on the Canada Council, in view of the fact that they form a substantial proportion of our population in western Canada.
The Ukrainian Canadians would greatly value your sympathetic attitude to our suggestions and your support for them when the time for their realization will come.
I hope the Prime Minister will not consider it too strong a term if I say that I think to some extent he committed himself in a speech he made on July 8, 1953, in the city of Winnipeg, when he addressed the all-Canada congress of Ukrainian Canadians, in which he made reference to the culture of this and other ethnic groups and concluded by saying, and I quote his own words:
It is only by taking an active part in all aspects of Canadian life, of giving as well as receiving, that any group can make a contribution to that Canadian life.
I could quote other parts of the Prime Minister's speech which are equally interesting and informative, but I think the right hon. gentleman will recall that he did say on that occasion that all ethnic groups in Canada should make their contribution to the Canadian culture we hope will evolve as a synthesis reflecting the new way of life of people of our nation.
I recommend these requests to the Prime Minister. I suggest to him that in some way, which of course cannot be placed in the bill itself, the requests of the Ukrainian Canadians be realized. They will be glad to lend their assistance in working closely with the Canada Council so that the information which as a matter of course will go to the English and French language press and other facilities for publication and publicity will also be

Canada Council
made available to foreign language newspapers, which are quite numerous and influential and are read in one language or another by approximately 20 per cent of the Canadian population. One person out of every five reads one or another of these foreign language newspapers.
I hope the Prime Minister will find a way of making use of this ethnic press club and the newspapers represented by them for the dissemination of information to the general reading public to whom they address themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to discuss this bill at this time, but in view of the many charges which have been hurled at members of this group I feel it is necessary for me to take some part in the discussion.
I would first question the members who have charged that we are opposed to culture. It is my understanding that to live is culture. I do not know how any man or woman in this house or in this country could be here and not have imbued in him or her some form of culture, whether it be representative of the ethnic culture we heard about a moment ago or the culture of the labourer from Regina city or the culture of any home in which we live or which we have occasion to visit.
Sometimes the culture within this house drops to a very low ebb indeed. I might speak for myself, as somebody suggests, but if I have in any way brought discredit on the house I would be the first to regret and acknowledge it. However, I do not think such is the case. Nevertheless, we have here an indication that nobody in this nouse requires subsidized culture. We do not require a culture that is fostered from without but, rather, a culture that is fostered from within.
The hon. member for Greenwood earlier today referred to what are, I believe, two of the most important factors with respect to culture; that is, truth and beauty. As I listened to him I wondered if we were prepared to recognize that what there is in art, what there is behind art itself, stems from the climate and events of ordinary life. We have heard a reference to Elvis Presley, and there was a reference made to abstract art. I believe that culture represents truth and beauty, but these are qualities in the abstract rather than tangible qualities because I must ask myself, "What is truth?" and "What is beauty?" Is an abstract painting beautiful? It may be beautiful to some members of this house, while others may hold up their hands in horror at this form of art. Yet it depicts a truth, a truth of the age in which we live, a truth of the atomic age, of
[Mr. Zaplitny.I
the fly by night efforts we have in this country today, of the disturbances which we see everywhere about us. Maybe that is what the abstract artist tries to capture and put on his canvas for all to see.
The question was raised by one of the hon. members of the Liberal party, are the antics of Elvis Presley culture? Certainly they are. They are culture, to some of us, of a low type; others of us, possibly not here, would consider them fine. Certainly they depict, just as abstract painting does, the age in which we live, the wild orgies that we read about in newspapers. And again we find that this is culture as an expression of life.
We in this group have been said to be opposed to culture. We are not opposed to culture. We just want the people of this country to have the privilege of developing their own culture. Our country is some 90 years old, now, and still we have not a flag. That is a form of culture; it is a part of culture, certainly. Money cannot buy a flag; it cannot buy devotion to duty or to a country. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that there are those who would see no beauty or truth in a dust storm. Yet if they had seen such a storm, as I have, they might be able to appreciate the horrible beauty and the terrible truth of the disaster which it can wreak upon prairie farms.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what kind of culture are we going to promote? That is the question which puzzles each and every one in this group. There are those in this country who have no desire to live hemmed in by mountains. There are others, myself included, who can appreciate the beauty of mountains. To one person they are beautiful; to another they may represent something quite different.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, an editorial from the Edmonton Journal based on a report by the Canadian Press and copied from the Vancouver Sun, dated October 30, 1956. The heading reads "Thriving Cultural Growth Shows Government 'Nursemaid' Not Essential". It is possible that the Prime Minister has seen this editorial, but maybe other members of the house have not, and there are parts of it which I believe to be worthy of consideration. The article says in part:
The council would apparently be a nursemaid for Canadian culture, empowered by the government to distribute money drawn from the taxpayers' pockets. The report is that it would have an endowment of between $50 million and $100 million-no mean sums even on a national scale.
While the project is favoured in some circles in Canada there will be grave misgivings about it in many minds. This applies particularly to the plan for distributing money to aid the development of Canadian arts.
This editorial was written considerably before the beginning of this debate. Surely,

Mr. Speaker, we must recognize in this portion of the editorial the fact that the people of this country as a whole are disturbed to think that this or any government would set itself out to decide what should be promoted in the way of culture. Reference has been made to the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, and to other provinces, and to the institutions they have set up. But none of them has proposed in any way to determine what should or should not be done in the direction of fostering culture.
